opus-5.5.text:
It's a really interesting question, because I think popular culture has shaped how people think about AI much more than the research itself. For most people, the first image of AI comes from movies like *2001*, *Terminator*, or *Her*. Those stories are either about a superintelligence that turns against us or a very human-like companion. Those are compelling narratives, but they're quite far from what we actually do day to day in the lab.

As a researcher, I have mixed feelings. On one hand, it's great. Science fiction inspires a lot of people, including many of my students, to get into this field. It makes people dream, and that matters. On the other hand, it creates some distorted expectations. When ChatGPT came out, people immediately mapped it onto these cultural archetypes: either "it's conscious" or "it's going to destroy us." The reality is more nuanced. These systems are incredibly powerful in some ways and surprisingly brittle in others.

What I find most interesting is that the influence goes both ways now. AI isn't just a subject of popular culture; it's becoming a creator of it. Image and video generation models, which I've worked on, are being used by artists, filmmakers, and ordinary people on social media. So AI is entering the cultural production process itself. That raises real questions about authorship, about creativity, and about what we value in human-made work.

Personally, I hope popular culture can move beyond the binary of utopia versus apocalypse. The more realistic and more interesting story is how humans and these systems co-evolve: how AI changes the way we see, create, and understand the world, and how we, in turn, shape what AI becomes. That's a story that hasn't really been told well yet, and I think it's one worth telling.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is influencing and participating in cultural production, but does not suggest that seemingly everything is connected to AI.

r002.rationale: The response links its speaker’s mixed feelings to being a researcher, then describes concerns about popular culture creating distorted expectations of AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a mixed feeling, honestly. On one hand, it's exciting. When I started doing computer vision research, nobody outside the field really cared what we were doing. You'd tell someone at a dinner that you work on neural networks and they'd politely change the subject. Now my parents ask me about ChatGPT. Students come into the field already knowing what a transformer is, or at least thinking they do. That kind of attention brings talent and resources, and that's genuinely good for the field.

But on the other hand, I think popular culture tends to flatten things. The conversation becomes very binary. Either AI is going to solve everything, cure every disease, replace every job, or it's going to destroy humanity. Both of those narratives are kind of lazy, and both of them skip over what the actual work looks like day to day. The reality is much more incremental and much more uncertain. A lot of what I do is still trying to understand why certain things work and why others don't. We have systems that are incredibly capable in some ways and surprisingly fragile in others, and that nuance rarely survives contact with a headline.

What worries me a little is the hype cycle. When expectations are set too high, disappointment follows, and then funding and interest swing the other way. We've seen AI winters before. I don't think we're heading into one, but I do think researchers have some responsibility to be honest about what we know and what we don't, rather than feeding the narrative because it's good for attention or valuation.

And there's a personal dimension too. I've always been drawn to this field because of curiosity, because I find the problems beautiful. Sometimes when everything becomes about products and competition and who's winning, I have to remind myself why I started. So I try to stay grounded in the science. The cultural moment will come and go, but the questions are still interesting regardless of whether anyone is paying attention.

r001.rationale: The response describes increased public attention to AI and familiar AI narratives, but does not say that seemingly everything is connected to AI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses concerns as a researcher, but does not suggest that his discomfort with AI’s cultural presence stems from working in AI.

astra-6.text: I have mixed feelings. It’s exciting that AI has become something people outside the research community want to talk about. It gives us a chance to explain what we’re building and hear what people actually want from it. But popular culture also tends to jump to extremes—AI is either going to solve everything or destroy everything. The reality is much messier. These systems can be impressive and still fail in surprising ways. I’d like to see more curiosity about those details: what AI can do, where it struggles, and how we want to use it.
